text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The jobs of the future will be created in the private service sector, and Swedes must be prepared to discuss higher wage differentials in Sweden if this is needed to create a labour market for cleaning, child-minding and other household services, the chairman of white collar union TCO says.

- A government cash bail-out the the tune of 800 million crowns or bankruptcy are the only two alternatives for state owned vocational training group AMU in the wake of cutbacks in the number of training places. The government held a crisis meeting on the issue on Tuesday.

- Closing two nuclear power reactors in Sweden could increase electricity prices by twice as much as has previously been indicated. Years with low precipitation tend to increase power prices, a fact that the state energy commission has not taken account of.
- Tennis ace Stefan Edberg made a tearful farewell to his professional career as he was knocked out in the first round of the Stockholm Open by compatriot Nicklas Kulti.
- Culture Minister Marita Ulvskog has been forced to back down from her plans to move three Stockholm museums to Gothenburg after a storm of public protest.
- Swiss-Swedish engineering group has lost a high-voltage transmission order to a value of 1.5 bilion crowns. ABB was unable to match Siemens' bid after the final tender round.
- Sweden has signed a double taxation agreement with Luxembourg, which will hit Swedish companies with subsidiaries in the principality and certain types of holding company.
Investors in private share funds are also affected by the changes, newsletter Early Warning reports.
- The Federation of Swedish Industries is to depart from its traditional strong ties with the forest, steel and engineering industries. Service companies are now welcome into the fold.
